729.title: Speak, for I hear (1 Samuel 3)
729.hook: the boy hears his name at night and answers "Speak; for Thy servant heareth"
729.howItsDone: Jews read Samuel's night call as part of the Former Prophets, and the boy's answer, speak, for thy servant heareth, is read as a picture of what it means to listen for God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah's song, the mighty falling and the poor lifted and seated among princes. Your line was raised from the dust. Who did you give a seat to? Today, her son, asleep in the sanctuary. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

It's night in the sanctuary at Shiloh. The old priest Eli is lying down in his place; his eyes have grown dim. The lamp of God hasn't gone out yet. And the boy Samuel is asleep near the ark. Then a voice says his name. Samuel. He jumps up, runs to Eli: here am I, you called me. Eli says, I didn't call. Lie down again. He lies down. The voice comes again. He runs again. Eli sends him back again. And the text slips in a quiet explanation: Samuel did not yet know the LORD. The word had never been revealed to him. He's hearing a voice he has no way to recognize.
screen: `NIGHT. THE LAMP STILL BURNS.` → `HERE AM I, YOU CALLED ME.` → `HE DIDN'T KNOW THE VOICE YET.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens with a sentence that sets the scene: in those days, the word of the LORD was rare, and visions were not common. So when it finally comes, it comes to a boy who can't tell it from an old man's voice. When the call comes the third time, Eli understands. And here's what the old priest does well. He doesn't take over. He doesn't say, let me handle this. He teaches the boy one sentence and sends him back to bed: if you are called, say, Speak, LORD; for Thy servant heareth. The voice comes, and this time, the text says, the LORD came and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. And Samuel answers, "Speak; for Thy servant heareth." Notice that the answer isn't a request. It isn't, give me a sign, or, tell me what I want. It's, I'm here, I'm listening, go ahead. And what he hears is hard. The message is about Eli's own house, judgment on his sons. Samuel lies there until morning, afraid to tell the man who raised him. Eli makes him tell everything, and hide nothing. And Eli answers: it is the LORD; let him do what seems good to him. So the night has two listeners. A boy learning to say speak, and an old man who hears bad news about himself and doesn't look away. The chapter ends with Samuel growing up, and the LORD letting none of his words fall to the ground. The rare word isn't rare anymore. It started with a boy in the dark, saying: speak.
screen: `THE WORD WAS RARE IN THOSE DAYS.` · `ELI TEACHES HIM ONE SENTENCE.` · `A HARD MESSAGE, TOLD WHOLE.` · `NONE OF HIS WORDS FELL TO THE GROUND.` · then, large: `SPEAK; FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen in the quiet. Tonight, or right now if it's quiet where you are, lie or sit still, and turn the lights down if you can. Don't ask for anything. Just listen. The fridge. A car. Your own breath. Your own thoughts, as they come. If something keeps coming back, a name, a worry, a person you owe a call, let it come. If you pray, you can say Samuel's words, speak, for thy servant heareth, and then stay quiet. If you don't, simply say to yourself: I'm listening. The bell holds the time.
Speak. The word Samuel says in the dark at Shiloh, taught to him by Eli, after he'd heard his name called three times: speak, for your servant is listening. Today's word.
Your line: here am I. Today, when someone starts to tell you something hard, say some version of it: go ahead, I'm listening. Then actually listen. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

what it means: in days when the word was rare, a boy learns to answer, listen, and tell a hard message whole.
what a scholar hears: Eli taught him to say speak, LORD; Samuel answers just speak; for thy servant heareth, without the name.

730.title: The glory departed (1 Samuel 4)
730.hook: the ark is captured, Eli dies, and a baby is named "the glory is departed"
730.howItsDone: Jews read the loss of the ark at Aphek as part of the Former Prophets, and some readers take the elders' plan to carry the ark into battle as a warning against treating holy things as charms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy in the dark at Shiloh, learning to answer. Your line was here am I. Did you let someone tell you something hard, all the way through? Today, the hard message comes true. Day seven hundred thirty.

A runner comes from the battlefield with his clothes torn and earth on his head. He runs straight into the city, and the whole city cries out. Eli, very old now, his eyes set so that he cannot see, is sitting on his seat by the road, waiting. His heart, the text says, trembled for the ark of God. Israel had lost a battle against the Philistines, and the elders had a plan: bring the ark of the covenant from Shiloh into the camp, so that it may come among us and save us. When it arrived, the soldiers shouted so loud the earth rang. Now the runner reaches the old man. Israel has fled. Your two sons are dead. And the ark of God is taken.
screen: `A RUNNER WITH EARTH ON HIS HEAD.` → `BRING THE ARK, IT WILL SAVE US.` → `THE ARK OF GOD IS TAKEN.`

segments.voice: It's the ark that breaks him. When the runner names the ark, Eli falls backward from his seat by the gate, his neck breaks, and he dies. And then the chapter does something unexpected. It doesn't stay with the generals or the priests. It goes to a woman in labor. Eli's daughter-in-law, the wife of his son Phinehas, is about to give birth. She hears all of it at once: the ark taken, her father-in-law dead, her husband dead. And the labor comes on her suddenly. The women attending her try to comfort her: fear not, you've borne a son. The text says she didn't answer, and didn't take it to heart. She has one thing left to do. She names the child Ichabod, saying, "The glory is departed from Israel." And the text says why: because the ark of God was taken, and because of her father-in-law and her husband. Then she says it again, as if once weren't enough: the glory is departed from Israel; for the ark of God is taken. Sit with what happened here. The elders carried the ark into battle so that it would save them. It didn't. The chapter doesn't soften it. In one day the ark is gone, the old priest at the gate is dead, and his two sons with him, and the one who names it plainly is a dying mother giving her son a name nobody would want. And yet the book doesn't end here. In the chapters that follow, the ark's story goes on, and it doesn't go the way the Philistines expected.
screen: `THE ARK CARRIED INTO BATTLE.` · `ELI FALLS AT THE GATE.` · `A MOTHER NAMES WHAT WAS LOST.` · `THE STORY DOESN'T END HERE.` · then, large: `THE GLORY IS DEPARTED FROM ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a loss of something grand. Not a small disappointment. Something bigger than you that you counted on. A place that closed. A community that broke apart. A hope you carried for years. A version of a family, or a country, or yourself. Settle, and let it come to mind. Don't rush to the bright side. Do what Phinehas's wife did, and give it a true name, even just in your head. Say what's gone. Then breathe, and let the naming be enough for now. If you pray, you can bring that loss to God exactly as it is. The bell holds the time.
Ichabod. The name a dying mother gives her son on the day the ark is taken and Eli dies, explained by her own words: the glory is departed from Israel. Today's word.
Your line: name it plainly. Today, if someone tells you about something they've lost, don't hurry them toward the bright side. Let them name it. Day seven hundred thirty.

731.title: Like all the nations (1 Samuel 8)
731.hook: the people ask for a king like everyone else, and Samuel warns them
731.howItsDone: Jewish commentators differ on this chapter: some read the request for a king as wrong in itself, others read Deuteronomy as allowing a king and fault only the people's motive, to be like the nations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mother naming her son Ichabod on the day the ark was taken. Your line was name it plainly. Did you let someone name a loss without hurrying them? Today, years later, the people want something new. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

Samuel is old now. He has judged Israel for a lifetime, going round a circuit from town to town, and he has made his sons judges after him. It doesn't work. His sons, the text says, did not walk in his ways. They turned aside after gain, took bribes, and bent justice. So the elders of Israel gather and come to Samuel at his home in Ramah, and they put it plainly. You are old. Your sons don't walk in your ways. And then the request: now make us a king to judge us, like all the nations.
screen: `SAMUEL IS OLD.` → `HIS SONS TAKE BRIBES.` → `MAKE US A KING.`

segments.voice: Notice that their complaint is fair. Samuel's sons really are corrupt. The text says so before the elders do. But listen to the last phrase. Not just, give us a better judge. Like all the nations. They want to look like everyone around them. The thing displeases Samuel, and he prays. And the answer he gets is surprising. Listen to the people, God tells him: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected Me, that I should not be king over them. And still, give them what they ask. But warn them first. So Samuel tells them what a king will do. He will take your sons for his chariots and his horsemen, to run before his chariots, to plow his ground and reap his harvest and make his weapons. He will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks and bakers. He'll take your best fields and vineyards and give them to his servants, and a tenth of your grain and your flocks. Listen to the verb. Take, and take, and take. And you, he says, will be his servants, and you'll cry out on that day because of the king you chose. Then the people answer, and they could not be plainer. No; but we will have a king over us; that we also may be like all the nations, that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles. They've heard the cost, and they still want it: a king to judge them and fight their battles, and to be like everyone else. God tells Samuel: listen to their voice, and make them a king. Some readers hear in this chapter a warning about power. Others hear something closer: how badly people can want to be like everyone else.
screen: `A FAIR COMPLAINT: CORRUPT SONS.` · `THEY REJECTED ME, NOT YOU.` · `TAKE, AND TAKE, AND TAKE.` · `WE WILL HAVE A KING ANYWAY.` · then, large: `THAT WE ALSO MAY BE LIKE ALL THE NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask why you want what others have. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've been wanting lately: a phone, a look, a car, a job title, a kind of vacation, a kind of life. Hold it for a moment. Then ask Samuel's question, gently. What will it take from me? Time, money, attention, freedom? And ask the elders' question, honestly: do I want it because it's good, or because everyone around me has one? You don't have to decide anything. Just see the reason clearly. The bell holds the time.
king. What the elders of Israel ask Samuel for, so they can be like everyone around them, even after he warns them what it will take. Today's word.
Your line: take, and take, and take. Today, the next time you reach for something because everyone has one, pause and ask what it will take from you. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

732.title: Hidden among the baggage (1 Samuel 10:20–24)
732.hook: the tall new king hides from his own crowning
732.howItsDone: Jews read Saul's choosing at Mizpah as part of the Former Prophets; commentators differ on whether his hiding shows humility or fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elders asking Samuel for a king, like all the nations. Your line was take, and take, and take. Did you catch yourself wanting something just because everyone has one? Today, they get their king, if they can find him. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

The whole people is gathered at Mizpah. Samuel is about to name a king, and he does it by lot, so everyone can watch it narrow down. The tribes come near, and the tribe of Benjamin is taken. Then the families of Benjamin, and the family of the Matrites is taken. Then one man: Saul, the son of Kish. Every eye turns to find him. And he isn't there. They look. They call. Nothing. So they do the only thing left, and ask the LORD: has the man come here yet? And the answer comes back: "Behold, he hath hid himself among the baggage."
screen: `BENJAMIN IS TAKEN.` → `SAUL, SON OF KISH.` → `AND HE ISN'T THERE.`

segments.voice: Here is what makes it strange. Saul already knows. Earlier, on the edge of town, Samuel took him aside and anointed him privately, poured oil on his head, and told him God had chosen him. When Saul went home and his uncle asked what Samuel had said, Saul told him about the lost donkeys he'd been chasing, and said nothing about the kingdom. And before any of that, when Samuel first hinted at it, Saul's answer was: am I not a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel, and isn't my family the least of them all? Gideon said much the same, down in his winepress. So when the lot falls on him in front of everyone, he can hardly be surprised. And he's hiding. Among the gear, the bags and supplies people brought with them. The tallest man in Israel, crouched behind the luggage. The people run and fetch him, and the text says that when he stood among them, he was higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward. Samuel says: do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There's none like him. And the people shout: long live the king. But not everyone. Some worthless men say, how shall this man save us? They despise him and bring him no gift. And Saul, the text says, held his peace. Readers have heard Saul's hiding in different ways. Some hear humility, a man who didn't want power. Some hear fear, a man who knew how heavy it would be. The text doesn't decide for us. It just shows a man who looked like a king from the outside, crouched where no one could see him.
screen: `ANOINTED IN SECRET, TOLD NO ONE.` · `THE SMALLEST OF THE TRIBES.` · `THE TALLEST MAN, BEHIND THE BAGS.` · `HOW SHALL THIS MAN SAVE US?` · then, large: `HE HATH HID HIMSELF AMONG THE BAGGAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the role you're hiding from. Settle, and breathe. Is there something you've been asked to do, or know you're meant to do, that you keep ducking? Leading something. Speaking up. Being the grown-up in a hard family moment. Taking the job, or the call, or the responsibility. Find it, and notice where you've been hiding: busyness, jokes, other people's needs, the luggage. Don't force a decision. Just stand up from behind the bags for a moment, in your mind, and let yourself be seen. If you pray, you can ask for the strength to stand. The bell holds the time.
Saul. The tall new king, already anointed in secret, found hiding among the baggage when the lot fell on him at Mizpah. Today's word.
Your line: he hid among the baggage. Today, accept one role you fear, even a small one: say yes to the thing you've been ducking. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

733.title: To obey is better (1 Samuel 15:22)
733.hook: "to obey is better than sacrifice"; Saul chose the showy offering
733.tomorrow: The Lord looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7)
733.howItsDone: Jews read Saul's war with Amalek as part of the Former Prophets, and Samuel's line that to obey is better than sacrifice is studied as a teaching about what God asks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tall new king crouched behind the luggage at Mizpah. Your line was he hid among the baggage. What role did you stop hiding from? Today, Saul is king, and he's not hiding anymore. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

"Blessed be thou of the LORD; I have performed the commandment of the LORD." That's how Saul greets Samuel, coming back from war against Amalek. Job done, as far as he's concerned. He has even, the text mentions, set up a monument for himself on the way home, at Carmel. And Samuel stands there and asks one quiet question. What then is this bleating of sheep in my ears, and the lowing of oxen that I hear? Because Saul had been told to leave nothing of Amalek's, and here are the best of the sheep and the cattle, alive, bleating, in the background of his victory speech.
screen: `I HAVE PERFORMED THE COMMANDMENT.` → `A MONUMENT AT CARMEL.` → `WHAT IS THIS BLEATING OF SHEEP?`

segments.voice: Saul has an answer ready. The people spared the best of the sheep and oxen, he says, to sacrifice to the LORD your God. The rest we destroyed. The command he was given against Amalek is hard to read, a command to destroy everything, and this lesson won't pretend otherwise. But the chapter's own question is narrower: Saul was told one thing and did another, then dressed it up as worship. And Samuel answers. Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt-offerings and sacrifices, as in hearkening to his voice? "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams." Listen to that pairing. To obey, and to hearken. In Hebrew, the word for obey here is the verb for hear, the same verb as in Shema, hear, O Israel. A few days ago, a boy in the sanctuary said speak, for thy servant heareth. Now a king is told that hearing is worth more than the fattest offering. Then Saul admits something. I have sinned, he says, because I feared the people, and hearkened to their voice. He did hearken. Just to the wrong voice. And even then, as Samuel turns to go, Saul asks: honor me now, I pray, before the elders of my people. Even his apology wants an audience. The prophet Hosea sounds a similar note later: God desires mercy, and not sacrifice. But here it is one king, a monument, and some bleating sheep he hoped no one would hear.
screen: `THE BEST WAS SAVED FOR SACRIFICE.` · `OBEY MEANS HEAR.` · `I FEARED THE PEOPLE.` · `HONOR ME BEFORE THE ELDERS.` · then, large: `TO OBEY IS BETTER THAN SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do what's asked, not what's showy. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing someone has actually asked of you lately. A partner, a parent, a boss, a friend, your own body. Not the grand gesture you'd like to make instead, the gift, the big speech, the dramatic fix. The plain thing they asked for. The dishes, the phone call, the apology without a speech. Hold it in mind, and notice whether part of you would rather do something more impressive. Then choose the plain thing. If you pray, you can hold Samuel's words: to obey is better than sacrifice. The bell holds the time.
Shema. The Hebrew verb for hear and obey, the same word Samuel used when he told Saul that obeying is worth more than the fattest offering. Today's word.
Your line: do the plain thing. Today, do one thing exactly as someone asked, plainly, with no monument and no audience. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

screen: `DAY 733 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.`

734.title: The Lord looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7)
734.word: The Lord looketh on the heart
734.hook: the youngest shepherd is chosen, not the tall brothers
734.howItsDone: Jews read David's anointing in Bethlehem as part of the Former Prophets, and the line that God looks on the heart is studied as a teaching about not judging by appearances.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saul, the bleating sheep, and Samuel's answer. Your line was do the plain thing. Did you do one plain thing exactly as asked? Today, Samuel goes looking for the next king. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

A horn of oil, and a dangerous errand. Samuel is sent to Bethlehem, to the house of a man named Jesse, because God has chosen a king from among his sons. Samuel is afraid: if Saul hears, he says, he'll kill me. So he goes with a heifer, to offer a sacrifice, and invites Jesse and his sons. The first son walks in. Eliab, the eldest. And Samuel looks at him and thinks, surely this is the one. He looks like a king. He's tall. Last time, Israel got a king who stood head and shoulders above everyone. Samuel has seen what a king looks like. This must be him.
screen: `A HORN OF OIL, TO BETHLEHEM.` → `ELIAB WALKS IN.` → `SURELY THIS IS THE ONE.`

segments.voice: And God says no. Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. Then the line this chapter turns on: "for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." Even a prophet, even Samuel, judged by height. Then Jesse brings the next son, Abinadab. Not this one. Then Shammah. Not this one. The text says Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel, and to each one the answer was the same: the LORD has not chosen these. So Samuel asks a question that sounds almost funny: are these all your children? And Jesse says, well, there's still the youngest. He's out keeping the sheep. Nobody thought to call him in. He wasn't even in the room. Samuel says, send and fetch him; we won't sit down until he comes. So they wait, everyone standing, for a boy to come in from the field. And when David arrives, the text does something surprising. It describes him. Ruddy, with beautiful eyes, and good to look at. The same chapter that says don't look at appearances tells us he was handsome. Some readers find that a little joke in the text: the point was never that looks are bad, only that they aren't what God goes by. And God says: arise, anoint him, for this is he. Samuel takes the horn of oil and anoints him in the middle of his brothers, and the spirit of the LORD comes on David from that day forward. The brothers in the room are passed over, and the one left in the field is chosen.
screen: `EVEN SAMUEL JUDGED BY HEIGHT.` · `SEVEN SONS, AND NOT THESE.` · `THE YOUNGEST, OUT WITH THE SHEEP.` · `HANDSOME TOO, AND THAT'S NOT WHY.` · then, large: `THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look past one appearance. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've sized up by how they look, or sound, or dress, or what they do for work. Someone you've filed away quickly. It might be a coworker, a neighbor, a relative, or you, in the mirror. Hold their face in mind. Then set the outside aside and ask: what do I actually know about their heart? What have they carried? What have they done when nobody was watching? If you don't know, just notice that. If you pray, you can hold Samuel's lesson: the LORD looketh on the heart. The bell holds the time.
The Lord looketh on the heart. What God tells Samuel in Jesse's house, when the prophet is ready to anoint the eldest son: people see the outside; God sees the heart. Today's word.
screen: `THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the heart, not the height. Today, when you meet someone, notice your first judgment, and then go looking for one thing about them you can't see. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

735.title: David's harp (1 Samuel 16:14–23)
735.hook: David plays and Saul's dark mood lifts
735.howItsDone: Jews read David's playing for Saul as part of the Former Prophets; by tradition, David is also linked with the book of Psalms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord looketh on the heart: the youngest son, called in from the sheep and anointed in Bethlehem. Your line was the heart, not the height. What did you find in someone that you couldn't see at first? Today, the same chapter, in the palace. Day seven hundred thirty-five.

One verse says the spirit of the LORD came on David. The very next verse says it left Saul. And something else comes instead. The text calls it an evil spirit from the LORD, and it terrifies him. The king is in the dark, and his servants can see it. So they make a suggestion, the kind people still make for someone who's low. Let our lord command us, they say, to look for a man who can play the harp. When the dark comes on you, he'll play with his hand, and you'll be well. Saul says yes. Find me someone who plays well, and bring him to me.
screen: `THE SPIRIT LEAVES SAUL.` → `THE KING IS IN THE DARK.` → `FIND SOMEONE WHO CAN PLAY.`

segments.voice: One of the young men already knows someone. I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, he says: skillful in playing, a mighty man of valor, a man of war, prudent, good-looking, and the LORD is with him. So Saul sends to Jesse: send me David your son, who is with the sheep. And Jesse loads a donkey with bread, a skin of wine and a young goat, and sends his youngest son to the king. Pause on what's happening. Nothing in the text says Saul knows what happened in Bethlehem, where this boy was just anointed with oil among his brothers. And David walks into the palace not as a rival, but as a musician, to help the man whose throne he'll one day sit on. Then the text says something tender: Saul loved him greatly, and David became his armor-bearer. And Saul sends word to Jesse: let David stay with me, for he has found favor in my sight. Then the chapter ends with a picture. Whenever the spirit from God was upon Saul, David took the harp and played with his hand, and Saul found relief, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him. The Hebrew word for this harp is kinnor, a stringed instrument. The book doesn't tell us what he played, or whether there were words. Just that someone played, at the moment the dark came, and the king was well. This week we heard a boy say speak, a mother name what was lost, a people ask for a king, a king hide among the baggage, a king keep the showy offering, and a shepherd chosen for his heart. Today that shepherd sits down beside the king, and plays.
screen: `A SON OF JESSE WHO CAN PLAY.` · `THE RIVAL WALKS IN AS A HELPER.` · `SAUL LOVED HIM GREATLY.` · `THE DARK SPIRIT DEPARTED.` · then, large: `DAVID TOOK THE HARP, AND PLAYED WITH HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: play music for someone who's low. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person who's in a dark stretch right now. Then think of one piece of music that might reach them. A song they love. A song from a better year. Something quiet. You don't need to play an instrument. You can send it, play it in the car with them, hum it on the phone, sit with them while it plays. For now, just choose the song, and hear a little of it in your head. If you pray, you can hold that person before God while you listen. The bell holds the time.
David's harp. The kinnor the young shepherd played for Saul, so that when the dark came, the king was refreshed and well. Today's word, and the close of a week in Samuel.
Your line: music lifts. Today, send the song you chose to the person you thought of, with no speech attached. Day seven hundred thirty-five.
